A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MobilePortrait, and all 18 pages support reliable comparison of text, equations, figures, tables, and references. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix or embedded supplement.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.4 report original video- and audio-driven evaluations, mobile latency measurements, ablations, and qualitative experiments.

after.justification: The same original empirical evaluations, latency measurements, ablations, and qualitative results remain in Sections 4.1–4.4.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same mixed-keypoint motion model, residual optical flow, appearance knowledge, U-Net backbones, audio-to-motion pipeline, and training losses.

E1.justification: Training and evaluation datasets remain unchanged, including VFHQ, VoxCeleb2, CelebVHQ, TalkingHead1K, CCv2, and HDTF. The same video/audio, same/cross-identity, and challenging appearance/motion scenarios are evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains PIRender, FaceV2V, TPS, MCNet, and Real3D. Table 6 retains MakeItTalk, SadTalker, and Real3D; comparator membership in the other comparisons is also unchanged.

E3.justification: The test samples, 25 FPS preprocessing, 512-pixel resolution, metrics, training budgets, model configurations, and mobile-device benchmarks are unchanged. The abstract's FPS edit introduces no revised evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: The computational-scale analysis, motion and synthesis ablations, training-data ablations, and challenging-case visualizations remain unchanged in Tables 2–5 and Figures 4–5.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variation, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The same point-estimate reporting is retained.

E6.justification: The abstract revises the reported validated mobile speed from over 100 FPS to over 50 FPS. Tables 1–6 and the plotted and qualitative results are unchanged, including Table 2's latency measurements; this does not establish a measured slowdown.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of keypoints and motion generation and the six-term objective in Equation (1) are unchanged. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract lowers the headline speed threshold from over 100 FPS to over 50 FPS, although the introduction retains 100+ FPS. The central claims about real-time mobile avatars, computational efficiency, and video/audio support remain unchanged.

C2.justification: The interpretations of component benefits, quality-versus-computation tradeoffs, and the audio-to-motion module's baseline status remain unchanged. No substantive explanation or limitation is added.

D1.justification: Implementation disclosures remain identical, including keypoint counts, the MLP merger, segmentation and inpainting components, eight A100 GPUs, learning rate 0.002, and 60 training epochs. The project-page link is unchanged.

R1.justification: Both versions contain the same 40 references and related-work discussion. The positioning as the first real-time one-shot neural head avatar solution for mobile devices is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace 'achieves state-of-the-art performance' with 'matches state-of-the-art performance'; the abstract's FPS value and arXiv version/date stamp also change. There is no broader rewriting or restructuring.

P2.justification: All five figures and six tables retain their contents, captions, structure, and placement. Page layout is unchanged; visual differences are confined to the edited text and version/date stamp.

improvement.justification: The revision makes the abstract's speed statement more conservative and substitutes near-equivalent performance wording without changing supporting evidence. Table 2 still supports over 100 FPS for smaller configurations, and the introduction retains that claim. These edits do not materially improve or harm scientific support, clarity, or reproducibility.
